Many of the pictures are taken in the infrared or the ultraviolet, well beyond our puny human abilities, because the information about composition that is recoverable from spectroscopic data. To our eyes it would look bland, but color the pictures based on spectroscopy, and they become more exciting to look at. It's then possible to distinguish the different types of matter on the surface or in nebulous clouds. Color image sensors don't exist, you get color from digital cameras from a mask filter that makes a pixel only sense a particular color, red green or blue. This comes at a cost in resolution, a third less off the top of my head. This is why most nasa images are black and white. The have spectrometers to disperse light, or camera sensitive to different parts of the em spectrum to make these false color images, but the information is there. Think of the false colors as matter dependent where 1 color for water ice, another for dirt etc. Or how much light each region reflects because that's information too, a shinny area gets more white and duller area more black, and the reflectivity in between a rainbow of color.
